<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_pruned_first">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Linxi Xie   Lisong C. Sun   Ashley Neall   
Tong Wu   Shengqu Cai   Gordon Wetzstein
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Stanford University     NYU Shanghai     UNC Chapel Hill

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Extended reality (XR) demands generative models that respond to users’ tracked real-world motion, yet current video world models accept only coarse control signals such as text or keyboard input, limiting their utility for embodied interaction. We introduce a human-centric video world model that is conditioned on both tracked head pose and joint-level hand poses.
For this purpose, we evaluate existing diffusion transformer conditioning strategies and propose an effective mechanism for 3D head and hand control, enabling dexterous hand–object interactions.
We train a bidirectional video diffusion model teacher using this strategy and distill it into a causal, interactive system that generates egocentric virtual environments. We evaluate this generated reality system with human subjects and demonstrate improved task performance as well as a significantly higher level of perceived amount of control over the performed actions compared with relevant baselines.
The project website is at <a href="https://codeysun.github.io/generated-reality/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://codeysun.github.io/generated-reality/</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18422v1/teaser_final3.png" id="p2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/278;" width="685" height="278" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Generated reality is a concept that incorporates human-tracked data (left) into an autoregressive video generation model to enable immersive experiences (right). These generated virtual environments do not rely on laboriously designed 3D assets but are created in a zero-shot manner by the video generator. We explore diffusion transformer conditioning strategies for joint-level hand and head poses, identifying a hybrid 2D–3D strategy as the most effective approach. Our bidirectional attention-based video generator is distilled into a few-step autoregressive model, enabling interactive, human-centric experiences supporting dexterous hand–object interactions.</span></figcaption>
</figure><span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup>

    <sup id="footnote1a.2" class="ltx_sup">†</sup>Work done as a visiting researcher at Stanford.</span></span></span>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F2.20" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S0.F2.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Diverse generations.<span id="S0.F2.21.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Leveraging the implicit world knowledge of foundation video models, our system generalizes to diverse scenarios with complex interactions. Generated videos (top) are visualized with input hand conditioning overlaid. Note that, consistent with the pretraining data, input text prompts (below) are augmented with an LLM before being input into the model.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extended reality (XR)—encompassing virtual, augmented, and mixed reality—is crucial in healthcare and rehabilitation, education and professional training, design and engineering, as well as entertainment and media.
Despite its transformative potential across these domains, the creation of XR content remains difficult, laborious, and expensive due to the need for specialized expertise, complex development tools, and high production costs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Emerging video world models offer a powerful platform to address the challenge of content creation for immersive technologies. These large generative AI models are able to autoregressively generate close-to-photorealistic video at interactive framerates conditioned on actions or other signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Current video world models, however, remain limited in the types of conditioning signals they accept, often restricted to simple keyboard controls or text prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>. The limited control makes current world models ineffective as human-centric content generation tools for XR applications. Recent works have focused on conditioning on camera motion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> or full-body pose <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, showing promise in modeling interactive egocentric dynamics. However, these approaches lack the precision required to represent the detailed wrist and finger movements involved in dexterous hand–object interactions. As a result, it remains an open question how to effectively incorporate joint-level hand pose conditioning into video diffusion models. Furthermore, it is unclear which conditioning strategies best preserve hand fidelity, realism, and temporal coherence in video generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that next-generation world models could support truly embodied interactivity by effectively incorporating rich streams of tracked user data, including head and gaze direction, body pose, foot placement, hand and finger articulation, and full-body movement.
To this end, we develop a human-centric video world model that enables interactive content generation across both existing and yet-unimagined applications, with a focus on effective head and hand control (see Figure <a href="#S0.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
Specifically, we present the first systematic study of hand pose conditioning strategies in video diffusion models. We compare several representative approaches, including token concatenation, addition, cross-attention, ControlNet-style conditioning, and adaptive layer normalization, using metrics that evaluate visual quality and hand-pose fidelity. We find that a combination of 2D ControlNet-style conditioning and a 3D joint-level representation of hand poses injected via token addition is the most effective. Finally, we distill our head- and hand-conditioned video generation model into a causal, real-time architecture, achieving 11 frames per second with a latency of 1.4 seconds on a remotely streamed H100. We conduct a user study with this system, demonstrating significantly improved task performance on three different tasks and a substantially larger perceived sense of control by human subjects compared to relevant baselines.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our vision of generated reality could enable immersive learning, training, and exploration by allowing users to acquire skills, practice complex tasks without detailed models, and experience real or imagined environments in a zero-shot manner. It could support novel interactive media and real-time generative guidance through smart eyewear for diverse applications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our key technical contributions include:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct a <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">comprehensive ablation</span> study comparing hand pose conditioning strategies for video diffusion models, identifying a combination of 2D ControlNet-style conditioning and 3D joint conditioning as the most effective strategy. <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Our method outperforms baselines</span> on video quality, camera pose accuracy, and hand pose accuracy metrics.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We distill our camera- and hand-conditioned bidirectional teacher model into an <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">interactive, autoregressive student model</span> that runs at interactive frame rates. Using this model, we demonstrate <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">improved task accuracy</span> and <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">increased perceived control</span> in our user studies.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>From Video Generation to World Simulation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent progress in diffusion models has significantly advanced the field of video generation. Transformer-based bidirectional models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> utilize full spatiotemporal attention to generate realistic and temporally coherent sequences.
However, their bidirectional denoising requires access to the full sequences, limiting their use in interactive scenarios. To support causal prediction and long-horizon rollouts, autoregressive video models have been introduced <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>. These methods generate frames sequentially in a manner more consistent with real-world dynamics.
These advances in video generation have motivated the development of world simulators, whose goal is to predict the visual consequences of actions given the current state <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>.
Recent advancements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> illustrate how actions can be applied to guide visual outcomes. However, most of these existing approaches rely on coarse action vocabularies such as keyboard and mouse inputs or raw camera poses, which describe scene-level information adequately but do not enable dexterous hand–object interactions. This highlights the need for fine-grained embodied control signals in interactive egocentric video generation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18422v1/pipeline_v5.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/233;" width="685" height="233" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Pipeline of generated reality system.<span id="S2.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We track the head and hand poses of the user with a commercial headset. Hands are represented using the UmeTrack hand model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, which includes translation and rotation of the wrist as well as rotation angles for 20 finger joints per hand. Our conditioning strategy employs a hybrid 2D–3D mechanism, combining a 2D image of the rendered hand skeleton (purple box, bottom) and the 3D model parameters (purple box, top). Features extracted from these modules are combined with the head pose features via token addition and fed into the diffusion transformer (DiT). The diffusion model autoregressively generates new frames at time <math id="S2.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> using the last few generated frames as context in addition to the user-tracked conditioning signals.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Camera- and Hand-conditioned Generation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In generated virtual environments, camera and hand motions jointly determine how people perceive and interact with their surroundings, making both modalities essential control signals for egocentric world simulators. Camera-conditioned video generation has been extensively explored with various condition-injection strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. For instance, ReCamMaster <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> injects camera extrinsic parameters through a dedicated camera encoder; CameraCtrl2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> encodes Plücker rays and adds them element-wise to visual features before the DiT module; and AC3D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> adopts a more dynamic design by introducing camera embeddings via a ControlNet-style feedback branch.
In contrast, hand-conditioned video generation remains relatively underexplored. PlayerOne <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> adds body pose embeddings to visual tokens before the DiT backbone, while PEVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> extends adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) to inject pose information. However, both methods treat hands merely as part of the full-body pose, thereby limiting the granularity of hand control. InterDyn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> employs binary masks instead of pose parameters as conditioning signals, which, however, increases the ambiguity between hand size and depth. In this work, we systematically compare various joint-level hand-conditioning strategies and identify a novel hybrid 2D–3D strategy that outperforms baselines on relevant metrics. We then incorporate this strategy into a camera-controlled video generation model, distill it into an autoregressive video generator, and evaluate this with users in an immersive format.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we briefly review preliminaries on video diffusion models (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Preliminaries ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>). We then discuss hand pose representations and video model conditioning strategies, proposing a novel hybrid 2D–3D conditioning strategy (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Hand Pose-conditioned Video Generation ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>). We describe how to extend this framework to jointly condition on tracked head/camera poses, as well as joint-level hand signals (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Joint Camera and Hand Control ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preliminaries</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our study builds upon the Wan family of video generation models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, a latent video diffusion transformer capable of generating temporally coherent video from a single input image or text prompt. The model consists of a 3D variational autoencoder <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{D})</annotation></semantics></math> and a transformer-based diffusion model parameterized by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta</annotation></semantics></math>. Given an input latent <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{0}=\mathcal{E}(V_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{0}=\mathcal{E}(V_{0})</annotation></semantics></math>, the forward process follows the rectified flow formulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, where the noised latent is generated by linear interpolation:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}=(1-t)\,z_{0}+t\,\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}=(1-t)\,z_{0}+t\,\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">with timestep <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. The denoising process learns a velocity field <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\Theta}(z_{t},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\Theta}(z_{t},t)</annotation></semantics></math> that guides the transformation of noise back to data. The model is trained using a conditional flow matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, with objective:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,z_{0},\epsilon}\!\left[\left\lVert v_{\Theta}(z_{t},t)-u_{t}(z_{0}\mid\epsilon)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>CFM</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,z_{0},\epsilon}\!\left[\left\lVert v_{\Theta}(z_{t},t)-u_{t}(z_{0}\mid\epsilon)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the target velocity derived analytically from the forward process. At inference, a sequence of latent frames is recovered by integrating <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{\Theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{\Theta}</annotation></semantics></math> over time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the image-to-video (I2V) setting, the model is conditioned on an initial image <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> encoded as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{\text{img}}=\mathcal{E}(I_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mtext>img</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{\text{img}}=\mathcal{E}(I_{0})</annotation></semantics></math>. The transformer-based denoiser <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\Theta}</annotation></semantics></math> autoregressively predicts video latents <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{z^{(f)}\}_{f=1}^{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>F</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{z^{(f)}\}_{f=1}^{F}</annotation></semantics></math>, starting from <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{\text{img}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mtext>img</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{\text{img}}</annotation></semantics></math> and producing temporally consistent sequences. In the text-to-video (T2V) setting, the model is instead conditioned on a text prompt <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> encoded as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{\text{text}}=\mathcal{T}(p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mtext>text</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{\text{text}}=\mathcal{T}(p)</annotation></semantics></math> and starts the autoregressive generation from noise. The final video is reconstructed as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{V}=\mathcal{D}(z^{(1)},\dots,z^{(F)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>V</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{V}=\mathcal{D}(z^{(1)},\dots,z^{(F)})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Hand Pose-conditioned Video Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Conditioning strategies for video diffusion models have been widely explored, yet joint-level hand poses remain a challenging modality due to their high dimensionality and complex articulation.
We systematically study how to integrate hand poses into video diffusion transformers (DiT), focusing on two design choices:
(1) the hand pose <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">representation</span>, i.e., how to represent tracked user hands, and
(2) the <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">conditioning strategy</span>, i.e., how the conditioning information is injected into the generative model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hand Pose Representation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One option for the hand pose representation is a ControlNet-style pose video <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>. This representation is essentially a sequence of images that visualize the positions of human body joints and corresponding bones in the 2D pixel image space. In the context of egocentric hand conditioning, the video encodes a 2D hand skeleton rendered from the user’s viewpoint.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While a skeleton video representation serves as a control signal spatially aligned with the image space, it inherently lacks 3D information. In immersive applications, a hand pose representation with 3D information is crucial for interactive video generation: in isolation, a 2D skeleton video exhibits depth ambiguity and suffers from self-occlusion as overlapping components of the skeleton make the position of certain hand joints ambiguous.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A 3D-aware hand representation is required for dexterous manipulation without ambiguities. Relevant parametric hand models are well known <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> and usually model a hand pose as a 6 degree-of-freedom (DoF) transformation of the wrist along with rotation angles of each finger joint.
We refer to the wrist pose and local joint rotations collectively as hand pose parameters (HPP). Applying standard forward kinematics to the HPP analytically yields the full set of 3D poses for all joints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For compatibility with our training data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, we adopt the UmeTrack hand model, whose HPP consist of 20 joint angles describing hand articulation together with the wrist pose.
These HPP provide metric precision in depth and hand articulation, complementing the coarse but spatially grounded skeleton video representation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hand Pose Conditioning.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To effectively incorporate hand pose parameters into the generative backbone, we examine four widely used condition injection strategies:
(1) <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">token concatenation</em>, (2) <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">token addition</em>, (3) <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN)</em>, and (4) <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cross-attention fusion</em>.
A pretrained variational autoencoder with encoder <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> projects a hand-contained raw video <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> into the latent space,
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{r}=\mathcal{E}(V_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{r}=\mathcal{E}(V_{r})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times f\times c\times h\times w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times f\times c\times h\times w}</annotation></semantics></math> is the latent of the raw video and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\times w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\times w</annotation></semantics></math> denote batch size, frame count, channel dimension, and spatial size, respectively. We additionally extract the hand pose parameters of the same video, denoted as <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times f\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times f\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is the dimensionality of the HPP.
For token concatenation (1), we add additional input channels to the input convolutional layer and concatenate the embedded HPP features with the video latents along the channel dimension before patchification:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=\operatorname{patchify}\!\left([\;z_{r},\;\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)\;]_{\text{channel-dim}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:3.700em;" width="3.700em"><mi>patchify</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mtext>channel-dim</mtext></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=\operatorname{patchify}\!\left([\;z_{r},\;\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)\;]_{\text{channel-dim}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a lightweight motion encoder composed of 1D convolutional layers.
For token addition (2), conditioning is applied through element-wise addition of HPP embeddings to patch tokens:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=\operatorname{patchify}(z_{r})\;+\;\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>patchify</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=\operatorname{patchify}(z_{r})\;+\;\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">For AdaLN (3), the hand features modulate the activations within each DiT block through adaptive scale and shift vectors,
a method inspired by adaptive normalization in conditional transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=\alpha(H)\odot v_{r}+\beta(H)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=\alpha(H)\odot v_{r}+\beta(H)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha(H)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha(H)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta(H)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta(H)</annotation></semantics></math> are learned from <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\odot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the Hadamard product.
Finally, for cross-attention fusion (4), HPP embeddings serve as keys and values in motion-conditioned cross-attention layers injected after selected Transformer blocks,
following the after-block cross-attention design of recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{(l+1)}=x^{(l)}+\operatorname{CrossAttn}\!\big(x^{(l)},\,\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)\big)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:4.590em;" width="4.590em"><mi>CrossAttn</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{(l+1)}=x^{(l)}+\operatorname{CrossAttn}\!\big(x^{(l)},\,\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)\big)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hybrid 2D–3D Hand Pose Conditioning.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a hybrid conditioning scheme that combines ControlNet-style 2D skeleton videos with the 3D-aware HPP. This strategy combines the efficiency of ControlNet with the spatial awareness of HPP.
As shown in Sec. <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">token addition</em> yields the best performance among the evaluated pose injection approaches. We therefore incorporate HPP into the skeleton-based video control branch via element-wise token addition.
Specifically, a hand-contained raw video <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> and its corresponding skeleton video <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{c}</annotation></semantics></math> are encoded by the same VAE encoder <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.
We then concatenate the two latents in a channel-wise manner, and inject the HPP features using token addition:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=\operatorname{patchify}\!\left([\;z_{r},\;z_{c}\;]_{\text{channel-dim}}\right)\;+\;\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:3.700em;" width="3.700em"><mi>patchify</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mtext>channel-dim</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.280em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=\operatorname{patchify}\!\left([\;z_{r},\;z_{c}\;]_{\text{channel-dim}}\right)\;+\;\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This design allows the model to resolve depth and self-occlusion ambiguity while maintaining strong spatial grounding from the skeleton representation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Joint Camera and Hand Control</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In head-mounted display (HMD) formats, visual content must be generated dynamically based on user interaction. Therefore, the user’s viewpoint (camera), left hand, and right hand are foundational control signals for interactive video generation. Hand interaction enables intent-driven movement of generated objects, and viewpoint interaction enables the user to view the generated content from new perspectives. To support these interactions, we introduce a framework for <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">joint hand and camera conditioning</span>, enabling realistic egocentric video generation driven by natural user interactions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Quantitative comparison of hand-motion conditioning strategies.<span id="S3.T1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
We perform an ablation study on the Wan2.2 14B model, evaluating hand pose parameters (HPP), binary mask, skeleton video, and hybrid conditioning schemes. Results are reported for both video quality as well as 3D and 2D hand pose accuracy, where best results are highlighted as <span id="S3.T1.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#BFFFBF;">first</span> and <span id="S3.T1.7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E1FFA8;">second</span>. Our hybrid strategy using both 2D skeleton projection and 3D HPPs achieves the best accuracy while maintaining a competitive video quality. Note that the position errors here are in millimeters and Procrustes aligned. ControlNet* represents the use of pixel-level image conditioning, but we do not copy the DiT blocks as done in the original ControlNet implementation.
</span></span></figcaption>
<table id="S3.T1.8" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

</figure>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.T2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Quantitative comparison of joint hand and camera conditioning strategies.<span id="S3.T2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Compared with the camera-only and hand-only baselines, JointCtrl achieves the best overall performance across video quality, hand pose, and camera pose metrics. It maintains the highest visual quality while delivering competitive control accuracy for both hand and camera signals, relative to models specialized in a single modality. Translation and rotation errors are reported in meters and degrees, respectively.

<span id="S3.T2.6.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:58.3pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.6.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T2.6.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ours</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.6.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#BFFFBF;"><span id="S3.T2.6.5.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#BFFFBF;">18.60</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.6.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#BFFFBF;"><span id="S3.T2.6.5.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#BFFFBF;">0.2800</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.6.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#BFFFBF;"><span id="S3.T2.6.5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#BFFFBF;">0.6173</span></td>

<td id="S3.T2.6.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E1FFA8;"><span id="S3.T2.6.5.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E1FFA8;">12.81</span></td>

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Camera Pose Representation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Previous works on pose-conditioned video generation often infer camera poses implicitly from body kinematics. For example, PlayerOne <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> estimates rotation-only camera trajectories from head pose with exocentric videos, while
PEVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> models viewpoint change via body joint signals without explicitly modeling camera extrinsics.
In contrast, we directly exploit the built-in inertial sensors and egocentric cameras of modern HMD, which provide a 6-DoF camera pose in world space, including both rotation (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}</annotation></semantics></math>) and translation (<math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in\mathbb{R}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in\mathbb{R}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>).
This explicit camera representation enables the accurate modeling of the camera (or head) pose, making the generated video responsive to a user’s head motion.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Joint Conditioning Strategy.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We transform the 6-DoF camera poses into per-frame Plücker embeddings <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times f\times 6\times h\times w}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times f\times 6\times h\times w}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, which are then projected into the same shape as the patch tokens with encoder <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}_{\text{cam}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>cam</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}_{\text{cam}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We then apply element-wise addition over three components in the latent space: (a) video latents, (b) HPP embeddings, and (c) camera embeddings:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E8X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\operatorname{patchify}\!\left([\;z_{r},\;z_{c}\;]_{\text{channel-dim}}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:3.700em;" width="3.700em"><mi>patchify</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mtext>channel-dim</mtext></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\operatorname{patchify}\!\left([\;z_{r},\;z_{c}\;]_{\text{channel-dim}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E8Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle+\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)+\mathcal{E}_{\text{cam}}(P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>conv</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mtext>cam</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle+\mathcal{E}_{\text{conv}}(H)+\mathcal{E}_{\text{cam}}(P)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The fused representation <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is then passed into the DiT blocks for generation. During training, both hand and camera signals are jointly optimized under a unified conditioning schema, ensuring coherent motion alignment between user actions and egocentric viewpoint changes. An overview of this joint conditioning architecture is shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 From Video Generation to World Simulation ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Iterative Encoder Training.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we find jointly training both encoders from scratch to be unstable. We attribute this to (1) both camera and HPP embeddings being added in the same operation and (2) ambiguity between motion caused by hand interaction and camera movement. Thus, we adopt an iterative training approach: camera and HPP encoders are first trained independently, with the camera encoder weights initialized from the FUN model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. Then, both encoders are trained jointly in a final fine-tuning step to merge the conditionings.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Qualitative comparison of hand-pose conditioning strategies.<span id="S3.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Ground-truth conditioning hand input is shown in red. Predicted hands are orange; overlap is green. Our hybrid conditioning strategy is most accurate among these baselines, especially when hands are partly occluded at the boundaries of the frame.</span></span></figcaption>

<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementation details.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building upon the Wan2.2 14B image-to-video (I2V) generation model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, we first conduct a systematic study to determine the most effective hand motion conditioning strategy.
Experiments are performed on the HOT3D dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, which captures hand–object interactions with precise 3D hand annotations obtained via optical-marker motion capture and synchronized camera pose annotations.
We segment each video into 5-second clips, yielding 5824 training samples, and reserve an unseen sequence of 45 clips for evaluation.
For each of the conditioning strategies described in Sec. <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Hand Pose-conditioned Video Generation ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we train LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> modules with rank 32 on both low-noise and high-noise experts for over 1K steps at a resolution of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="480\times 480" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>480</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>480</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">480\times 480</annotation></semantics></math>, using a learning rate of <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> and a batch size of 16.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our model along three dimensions: overall video quality, hand pose accuracy, and camera pose accuracy. For video quality, we report PSNR for pixel-level accuracy, LPIPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> for perceptual similarity, SSIM for structural consistency, and Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) for distribution-level realism.
For hand pose accuracy, we use WiLoR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> to evaluate Procrustes Aligned Mean Per-Joint Position Error (PA-MPJPE) computed over 20 joints to measure 3D pose accuracy, and Procrustes Aligned Mean Per-Vertex Position Error (PA-MPVPE) computed over 778 vertices to measure 3D hand shape accuracy. We further compute the average L2 distance between ground truth and generated hand landmarks in the pixel space of each 2D frame <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. Camera pose accuracy is evaluated by extracting estimated trajectories from generated clips using GLOMAP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> and computing rotation error (RotErr) and translation error (TransErr) following previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluating Hand-pose Conditioning.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Among the four injection strategies evaluated for conditioning on hand pose parameters (HPP), the <em id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">token addition</em> method achieves the best performance across hand pose accuracy metrics, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Joint Camera and Hand Control ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
In contrast, <em id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cross-attention</em> and <em id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">AdaLN</em> struggle to establish a stable mapping between HPP and visual features, likely due to the limited scale of the HOT3D dataset and the high dimensionality of the HPP, performing worse than the unconditioned baseline.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Qualitative comparison of joint hand–camera control.<span id="S4.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Ground-truth (GT), camera-only, hand-only, and joint-control results.
Camera-Ctrl and Hand-Ctrl are effective at controlling one of these modalities but not the other.
Our Joint-Ctrl mechanism enables simultaneous control of camera and hands.</span></span></figcaption>

</span></span>
