</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate hybrid conditioning that integrates both skeleton video and HPP information.
As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Joint Camera and Hand Control ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the hybrid approach achieves the best performance across all hand accuracy metrics.
Although the numerical gains over the ControlNet-style 2D skeleton-image conditioning strategy are moderate, likely due to the relatively simple hand motions in HOT3D, the hybrid 2D–3D method still produces more stable and anatomically faithful hand reconstructions qualitatively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To contextualize the quantitative results for hand pose accuracy, we estimate lower bounds for the different metrics by evaluating the HOT3D test annotations under the same protocol, i.e., by fitting a 3D hand model using WiLoR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> to the ground truth test images and evaluating our hand pose accuracy metrics.
This yields MPJPE of 9.42, MPVPE of 7.74, and an L2 landmark error of 9.08,
representing the inherent accuracy and uncertainty of the WiLoR-based hand pose estimator we use for all generated frames. Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Joint Camera and Hand Control ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (right) shows that our hybrid conditioning method approaches this lower bound. To further validate robustness beyond HOT3D, we evaluate on the larger GigaHands dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> and observe consistent improvements over 2D-only conditioning (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Alternative Datasets ‣ Appendix B Additional Evaluation ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Qualitative comparisons in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Iterative Encoder Training. ‣ 3.3 Joint Camera and Hand Control ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> highlight these improvements, where predicted hands are shown in orange, ground truth in red, and their overlap in green.
In the challenging case shown in this figure, ControlNet conditioning fails to reconstruct hands near the image boundary due to incomplete skeleton inputs, whereas the hybrid model generates complete and spatially consistent hand structures even when hands are close to the frame edge.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluating Joint Head- and Hand-pose Conditioning.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the proposed joint hand–camera conditioning framework against hand-only (HandCtrl) and camera-only (CameraCtrl <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>) baselines.
As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Joint Camera and Hand Control ‣ 3 Conditional Video Generation with Tracked Head and Hands ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the joint-control model achieves the best video quality and balanced performance across hand and camera pose metrics.
Specifically, CameraCtrl achieves the lowest rotation and translation errors in camera pose but fails to maintain accurate hand alignment, whereas HandCtrl produces precise hand poses but lacks camera control.
Our joint-control model bridges this gap, achieving coherent coordination between hand motion and head dynamics.
Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Evaluating Hand-pose Conditioning. ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> further illustrates that, without camera control, the hand-only model often interacts with incorrect objects.
In this example, the hand-only model incorrectly predicts user intent by reaching toward an object on the table instead of the cup on the left.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>The Generated Reality System</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using our detailed analysis of joint-level hand- and head–conditioned video generation, we next develop our generated reality system. This is a variant of the aforementioned video diffusion model, rolled out in a causal, i.e., autoregressive, manner and distilled to achieve interactive frame rates. The user’s head and hand poses are dynamically tracked with a commercial VR system and used to condition the video generation model, whose output is streamed directly to the headset worn by the user.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Autoregressive Distillation.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the self-forcing strategy, we distill a bidirectional Wan2.2 5B teacher model that is trained with our head- and hand-conditioning strategy into a causal 5B student model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. Autoregressive videos are generated in 12-frame chunks, complete with per-frame hand and head conditioning as outlined. The model supports both image-to-video (I2V) and text-to-video (T2V) settings.
The resulting system provides a closed-loop generative experience—users can continuously move their hands and head, and the model renders the corresponding virtual response.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Integration with VR System.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A real-time generative VR system is implemented with Unity on the Meta Quest 3. We use the captured head and hand poses from the Quest as our conditioning. This conditioning is streamed to a server hosting the distilled autoregressive model. For each video chunk, conditionings are read from a circular frame buffer with the most recent tracked data. Generated video chunks are then streamed back to the Quest 3 for interactive viewing in VR. We achieve 11 FPS in real-time with 1.4 seconds of latency on a single H100 GPU. The latency is bottlenecked by the time to generate and decode a 12-frame chunk. The added conditioning adds only an additional 0.002 s of latency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">User Study Design.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate our generated reality system, we conducted two user studies. For this purpose, we recruited 11 subjects (age range = 22–30 years). The cohort consisted of 4 female and 7 male participants; 6 of them wore glasses. All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18422v1/figs/tasks.jpg" id="S5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/228;" width="685" height="228" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18422v1/figs/user_study_setup.jpg" id="S5.F6.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/381;" width="685" height="381" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">User study tasks and setup<span id="S5.F6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Our subjects completed three tasks using a commercial virtual reality headset: “push the green button”, “open the jar”, and “turn the steering wheel”. Representative screenshots of all three tasks from the perspective seen by the user (top). A photo of our setup, in which the generated video’s hands reflect the user’s in real-time (bottom).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We designed the three different environments shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ User Study Design. ‣ 5 The Generated Reality System ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> for our studies. Observing these in the Quest headset, we ask users to perform the following tasks: “push the green button”, “open the jar”, and “turn the steering wheel”, respectively. Users had a total of 8 seconds to complete a task. We tested two conditions for each task: one using our hand- and head-pose conditioned model and one baseline model that uses only head-pose conditioning. The relative difference between these conditions, therefore, demonstrates the effectiveness of hand control in our application. The baseline relies purely on the text-conditioned video model to complete the task without the user directly controlling the generated rendering of their hands. Users completed each of the three tasks four times (twice for each of the conditions), all in random order. Before starting each run, we asked users to roughly align their hands with the input image; we overlay their real-time hand pose to assist with this process. Once they indicated alignment, we disabled the hand pose overlay and began the interactive experience, so users saw only the environment, the generated hands, and the results of hand-object interactions. Users were allowed two practice runs to familiarize themselves with the process before we began recording results. More details are outlined in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C User Study Details ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18422v1/user_study.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/313;" width="685" height="313"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S5.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">User evaluation<span id="S5.F7.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. We show human subjects interactive videos without (baseline) and with (ours) tracked hand conditioning signals. For the baseline, we prompt the video model to complete the task using the same instructions provided to human subjects in our setting. In our tracked hand conditioning setting, users can more accurately complete the task than a video model can with just text conditioning (left). Moreover, users report a significantly higher level of perceived control over the interaction in our setting compared to the baseline, measured using a 7-point Likert scale (right). </span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluating Task Efficiency.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ User Study Design. ‣ 5 The Generated Reality System ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> (left), the baseline achieved an average of 3.0% for task accuracy, demonstrating that text prompts alone are insufficient for reliably completing tasks that require fine-grained hand–object interaction. Under identical conditions, our hand-controlled model achieved 71.2% task accuracy on average, highlighting the substantial improvement in task success provided by explicit hand controls.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluating User Experience.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After each trial, participants rated their perceived amount of control on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = worst, 7 = best). Shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ User Study Design. ‣ 5 The Generated Reality System ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> (right), our hand-controlled model received a mean score of 4.21, compared to 1.74 for the baseline. These results indicate that participants experienced markedly greater control over hand pose and movements with explicit hand conditioning than with text prompts alone, aligning with the observed improvements in task success.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present crucial first steps towards a vision of human-centric world simulation. Specifically, we identify and evaluate efficient and effective mechanisms for conditioning video diffusion models on tracked head and joint-level hand data. Moreover, we present a first version of an interactive generated reality system and demonstrate its efficacy with user studies.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The resolution, latency, stereo rendering capabilities, image quality, and computing efficiency of our system lag far behind those of modern virtual reality systems. As with all current autoregressive video models, drift significantly degrades the image quality after a few seconds of rollout. Yet, the promise of generating an interactive and immersive virtual environment in a zero-shot manner is unprecedented and motivates future research on solving these issues.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Future Work.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Improving the aforementioned limitations towards retinal image resolution in stereo with imperceptible (i.e., <math id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;20</annotation></semantics></math> ms) latency and long rollouts on a wearable computer embedded in a headset is an enormous challenge. Yet, most of these problems are well aligned with ongoing research and development efforts on autoregressive video diffusion models across the computer vision and AI communities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Conclusion.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generated reality could enable immersive learning and exploration, letting users acquire skills and practice complex tasks in a zero-shot manner, without the need for laborious modeling of 3D virtual environments.


<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Experiment Details</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Initialization of the Motion Encoder</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments are based on the Wan2.2 14B model family, which uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with two DiT experts: one specialized for high-noise steps and one for low-noise steps. To train the motion encoder effectively under this design, we adopt a continual training scheme.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">During high-noise DiT training, we zero-initialize the motion encoder. After convergence, the trained encoder is transferred and used as the initialization for low-noise training. This two-stage setup provides a stronger starting point for the low-noise model and mitigates the impact of the limited HOT3D dataset, resulting in more stable training and improved motion alignment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Continual Training of DiT Experts</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For hybrid conditioning, we aim to emphasize fine-grained alignment during training.
To achieve this, we initialize the DiT with the LoRA weights learned from skeleton-video conditioning and continue training from this point.
This provides the model with a well-structured spatial prior and allows the hybrid training stage to focus on refining articulation and depth cues introduced by the hand pose parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Similarly, for joint hand–camera conditioning, we initialize the DiT with the LoRA weights obtained from the hybrid model and then train with both hand and camera inputs.
This continual training strategy gives the joint model a strong initialization and leads to more stable convergence and improved motion consistency. Furthermore, it helps the model decouple the conditionings, which are both applied in the same token addition operation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Lower bounds</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We estimate the lower bound of our evaluation pipeline by running the same
metrics on the HOT3D validation annotations themselves.
Hand poses are obtained from WiLoR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, and camera trajectories are
computed using GLOMAP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.
This provides the inherent error level of the annotation and reconstruction
process under our evaluation protocol.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T3" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional Evaluation</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Alternative Datasets</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to HOT3D, we evaluate our method on the larger GigaHands <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> dataset (<math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="8\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger than HOT3D) with the Wan2.2 5B model. As shown in Table <a href="#A2.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ B.1 Alternative Datasets ‣ Appendix B Additional Evaluation ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we continue to yield consistent improvements over the baselines; particularly, our 2D–3D hybrid conditioning outperforms 2D only conditioning, reducing MPJPE by 10%, MPVPE by 11%, and 2D error by 34%. These results indicate scalability to larger, more complex data and richer hand motions. Fig. <a href="#A4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Appendix D Limitations ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> and <a href="#A4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Appendix D Limitations ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> provide additional qualitative comparisons across four scenes from the GigaHands dataset.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Text-to-Video Generation</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite being trained on videos from a controlled studio environment, our model is able to transfer its hand interaction capabilities to diverse scenes unseen in training. To demonstrate “human-centric” generation beyond HOT3D’s controlled hand-object interactions, we conduct text-to-video generation across complex, dynamic scenarios (Fig. <a href="#S0.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F8.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A3.F8.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">User Study Qualitative Comparison.<span id="A3.F8.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Captured user study results of the baseline vs. our method.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#A3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Appendix C User Study Details ‣ Generated Reality: Human-centric World Simulation using Interactive Video Generation with Hand and Camera Control" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> visualizes comparisons between baseline and our method, captured during the user study. We chose short, simple tasks to enable objective (binary) completion measures and to isolate controllability from generation complexity and long-horizon drift; this also reduces participant discomfort given the current latency.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After each recorded run, participants are asked the question: “On a scale from 1-7, with 1 being no control and 7 being full control, rate the perceived controllability of the system.”
To measure task completion, all generated videos from the session are blind-reviewed by a separate participant for a binary failure/success metric.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the system models complex hand-object interactions, it struggles with longer-range hand-object-object dependencies. The causal model suffers drawbacks typical of DMD distillation methods, i.e., mode-seeking behavior and over-saturation over long horizons.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We acknowledge that 1.4 second latency is not sufficient for fully immersive XR systems. However, this latency is not fundamental to our approach and can be improved with better hardware, alternative distillation methods, and system optimization (e.g., we communicate with a remote GPU server rather than a local one). Despite this concern, we believe the system to be a practical tool for rapid prototyping and open-ended creation.</p>
</div>
